brief.desc: BEARISH, 40/100. Gold just had its best week since late August, but it is still below both its 50-day and 200-day averages and down 3.1% over 20 sessions despite a roughly 30bp fall in the 10-year real yield. Friday's 165k payroll beat revived the December hike that drives the dollar and real yields; confidence is moderate and Tuesday's CPI decides it.
brief.yr: GLD closed at $372.52, down 0.79%, in a $369.26 to $373.76 range on November 6, with futures provisionally down about 0.95% near $4,075. October payrolls rose 165,000 against roughly 65,000 expected, unemployment fell to 4.1% and hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month. December hike odds rose to about 77% from 72.8% before the release and the dollar index jumped 0.72% to 102.28. GLD closed well off its lows, so dip buyers absorbed about half of the move.
brief.to: Base case (45%) is a retest of the late-October lows near $3,850 if Tuesday's October CPI prints 0.4% or more on the month and keeps December hike odds above 75%. A range of $3,950 to $4,150 (35%) needs an in-line CPI, and a breakout to about $4,250 (20%) needs a soft CPI that pushes hike odds below 50%. The week's other events are October PPI on Friday and Monday's first posting of post-payroll yields. This view flips bullish if the 10-year TIPS real yield prints below 2.50% and December hike odds fall below 50% after the November 10 CPI.

brief.why: The most informative fact in the data is a failure: over 20 sessions the 10-year real yield fell about 27bp, and GLD still lost 3.1% and broke to a 52-week low of $354.67 on October 30. Gold did not monetize its biggest driver. The level matters more than the change. At 2.60 to 2.64% real and a funds rate of 3.75 to 4.00% with hikes being priced, holding gold still costs a lot in real terms. The real-yield decline was itself a growth scare: nominal 10s fell from 5.24% to 4.84% while breakevens also fell, which helps bonds more than gold. The Fed is reacting to inflation that is hot and broadening, with September CPI at 3.7% and PPI at 6.3% year on year. It now has a labour market that just beat by 100k with wages up 0.4% on the month, and two October dissents for a hike say the committee is close to moving. Each strong print lifts the 2-year and the dollar, so the Fed path now drives real yields and the dollar, and both point the wrong way for gold. The buyers are official and price-insensitive, 321 tonnes in Q3. That sets a floor and explains the sharp reversal from October 30, but it does not set the marginal price day to day. Western ETF and futures money, still net long more than 100k contracts, does that. This week's bounce looks like short-covering and dip-buying into a real-yield move that has probably run its course.
brief.cons: The loud story is best week since August, central banks at a 2026 high, the bottom is in. The central-bank figure is real, but it is a quarterly demand fact being used as a timing signal. The crowded position is not a short. Managed money was still net long 104,206 contracts as of October 20, barely trimmed, even after GLD fell about 25% from its January high. If CPI firms up a December hike, that long is the fuel for a second leg down. The consensus also leans on the 10-year real-yield decline as bullish evidence, but gold's 20-day tape already rejected that argument. One point cuts against my call: ETF holdings were rising early in the week, so the bounce had some real buying behind it, and the positioning data is two and a half weeks old.
fals: Soften: GLD closes above its 50-day average of about $385 on any day through November 13; the downtrend would then be broken and the call moves to neutral.
Invert: after the November 10 CPI, the 10-year TIPS real yield (FRED DFII10) prints below 2.50% and December hike odds fall below 50% by November 13; the call becomes bullish.

Weak joint: I am assuming Friday's payroll beat pushed real yields and the 2-year higher, but Treasury had not posted November 6 rows at writing, so I find out Monday; the claim that managed money is still long rests on an October 20 COT print.
